item.title: The Creation of Adam
item.lesson: Michelangelo insisted he was a sculptor, not a painter, and tried to refuse the Sistine ceiling commission from Pope Julius II. Four years of labor later — standing on scaffolding he designed himself, paint dripping into his eyes — he had produced the most famous ceiling on Earth. In this panel, its center of gravity, God surges toward a languid Adam whose hand rises barely, not quite meeting his maker's. That gap between the fingers is the painting's genius: the entire drama of creation compressed into a few inches of empty plaster. Adam's body is pure sculpture in paint, a Greek god borrowed for Genesis. And because fresco must be painted onto wet plaster in day-sized patches, we know Michelangelo painted Adam's whole torso in a single day's session — one of the great single days of work in human history.
item.lookFor: Look at the swirling rose-colored mantle around God: many see the precise cross-section of a human brain in its outline — anatomy Michelangelo knew intimately from dissections, though whether he hid it there on purpose remains a delicious open question.
